subject: Physics
resource_text: Kinematics: Equations of uniformly accelerated motion: v = u + at, s = ut + (1/2)at^2, v^2 = u^2 + 2as. They apply only when acceleration is constant, and s is the signed displacement, not the distance travelled.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Kinematics: Projectile motion: horizontal velocity u cos(theta) stays constant while the vertical motion has acceleration -g. Time of flight T = 2u sin(theta)/g, maximum height H = u^2 sin^2(theta)/(2g), range R = u^2 sin(2theta)/g.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Kinematics: Relative velocity: v_AB = v_A - v_B as vectors. In river-boat problems the shortest crossing time is obtained by heading perpendicular to the bank; zero drift needs v_boat sin(theta) = v_river upstream.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Kinematics: On a velocity-time graph the slope is acceleration and the area under the curve is displacement. Area below the time axis is negative displacement; for distance add the absolute areas.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Kinematics: Motion under gravity: for free fall take g = 10 m/s^2 downward. Choose upward as positive and a = -g; at the top of the path v = 0. The time to rise equals the time to fall back to the same level.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Kinematics: Average speed is total distance over total time, while average velocity is displacement over time. For two equal distances covered at speeds v1 and v2, the average speed is 2 v1 v2/(v1 + v2), the harmonic mean.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Kinematics: Distance covered in the nth second by a uniformly accelerated body: s_n = u + a(2n - 1)/2. It is the displacement between t = n-1 and t = n, not the displacement up to t = n.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Kinematics: Horizontal projectile from a height h: time of flight t = sqrt(2h/g) and range R = u sqrt(2h/g). The horizontal speed stays constant while the vertical speed is gt.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Laws of Motion: Newton's second law: net force F = ma. Draw a free-body diagram, choose axes along the motion and write the sum of forces = m x a separately for each axis.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Laws of Motion: Friction: static friction adjusts up to f_s(max) = mu_s N; kinetic friction is f_k = mu_k N and acts opposite to motion. On an incline N = mg cos(theta) and the pull along the slope is mg sin(theta).

subject: Physics
resource_text: Laws of Motion: Connected bodies and pulleys: for a light inextensible string the tension is the same throughout and the bodies share the same acceleration magnitude. Atwood machine: a = (m1 - m2)g/(m1 + m2).

subject: Physics
resource_text: Laws of Motion: Newton's third law: action and reaction act on different bodies, so they never cancel in the free-body diagram of one body. In a lift accelerating upward with a, the apparent weight is m(g + a).

subject: Physics
resource_text: Laws of Motion: Momentum p = mv and Newton's second law in general form F = dp/dt. Impulse J = F dt equals the change in momentum; for a constant force J = F t.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Laws of Motion: Circular motion needs a centripetal force F = m v^2/r directed towards the centre. At the top of a vertical circle the minimum speed for a string to stay taut is sqrt(g r).

subject: Physics
resource_text: Laws of Motion: Pseudo force: in a frame accelerating with a, a body of mass m experiences a pseudo force -ma. In a lift accelerating upward the apparent weight is m(g + a); accelerating downward it is m(g - a).

subject: Physics
resource_text: Laws of Motion: Limiting friction and angle of repose: a block just begins to slide on an incline when tan(theta) = mu_s, so the angle of repose equals arctan(mu_s).

subject: Physics
resource_text: Work Energy Power: Work done by a constant force W = F d cos(theta). Work-energy theorem: net work = change in kinetic energy = (1/2)m v^2 - (1/2)m u^2. A force perpendicular to the motion does zero work.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Work Energy Power: Gravity and spring forces are conservative, so KE + PE stays constant when only they act. Spring energy is (1/2)k x^2 and gravitational PE near the Earth is mgh.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Work Energy Power: Power P = W/t = F.v. Average power uses total work over total time; instantaneous power uses the velocity at that instant. 1 horsepower is about 746 W.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Work Energy Power: An elastic collision conserves momentum and kinetic energy; in a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies stick together and only momentum is conserved. Momentum is conserved in every collision with no external force.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Work Energy Power: Work done by a variable force is the area under the F-x graph, W = integral of F dx. For a spring stretched from 0 to x the work done is (1/2) k x^2.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Work Energy Power: Power of a lifting machine or pump: P = m g h / t. Efficiency = useful output power / input power, and is always less than 1 for real machines.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Work Energy Power: Coefficient of restitution e = relative speed of separation / relative speed of approach. e = 1 for an elastic collision and e = 0 for a perfectly inelastic one.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Work Energy Power: Kinetic energy and momentum are related by KE = p^2/(2m). Two bodies with the same momentum have kinetic energies inversely proportional to their masses.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Rotational Motion: Torque tau = r F sin(theta) = I alpha. Moment of inertia: ring MR^2, solid disc (1/2)MR^2, solid sphere (2/5)MR^2, thin rod about its centre (1/12)ML^2.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Rotational Motion: Parallel axis theorem I = I_cm + M d^2 and perpendicular axis theorem I_z = I_x + I_y (flat bodies only). Check which axis is asked before choosing a formula.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Rotational Motion: Angular momentum L = I omega is conserved when the net external torque is zero. A skater pulling her arms in reduces I, so omega increases.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Rotational Motion: Rolling without slipping: v = omega R and total kinetic energy = (1/2)m v^2 + (1/2) I omega^2. Acceleration down an incline is a = g sin(theta)/(1 + I/(m R^2)).

subject: Physics
resource_text: Rotational Motion: Rotational kinematics mirrors linear motion: omega = omega0 + alpha t, theta = omega0 t + (1/2) alpha t^2, omega^2 = omega0^2 + 2 alpha theta. Linear and angular quantities relate by v = r omega and a_t = r alpha.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Rotational Motion: Rotational kinetic energy is (1/2) I omega^2. For rolling without slipping the total KE = (1/2) m v^2 + (1/2) I omega^2 with v = omega R.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Rotational Motion: Rolling down an incline without slipping: a = g sin(theta)/(1 + I/(m R^2)). A solid sphere has I/(m R^2) = 2/5, so a = (5/7) g sin(theta), which is less than a frictionless slide.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Rotational Motion: Centre of mass of a system: x_cm = (m1 x1 + m2 x2)/(m1 + m2). For two particles it lies on the line joining them, nearer to the heavier one.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Gravitation: Newton's law of gravitation F = G m1 m2 / r^2. Acceleration due to gravity g = GM/R^2 at the surface; at height h, g' = g (R/(R + h))^2; at depth d, g' = g(1 - d/R).

subject: Physics
resource_text: Gravitation: Gravitational potential energy of two masses is U = -G m1 m2 / r (zero at infinity). Escape velocity v_e = sqrt(2GM/R) = sqrt(2gR), about 11.2 km/s for the Earth.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Gravitation: Orbital speed for a circular orbit v = sqrt(GM/r); the time period obeys T^2 proportional to r^3 (Kepler's third law). Total energy of a satellite is -GMm/(2r).

subject: Physics
resource_text: Gravitation: Kepler's laws: planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus; the line to the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times (angular momentum conservation); T^2 is proportional to a^3.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Gravitation: Acceleration due to gravity g = GM/R^2 at the surface. At height h above it g' = g (R/(R + h))^2; at depth d below it g' = g (1 - d/R), which is zero at the centre.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Gravitation: Escape velocity v_e = sqrt(2GM/R) = sqrt(2gR), about 11.2 km/s for the Earth. It is independent of the mass of the escaping body and is sqrt(2) times the orbital speed near the surface.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Gravitation: Satellite energy: kinetic energy = GMm/(2r), potential energy = -GMm/r, total energy = -GMm/(2r). A bound orbit has negative total energy whose magnitude equals the kinetic energy.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Gravitation: A geostationary satellite has a period of 24 h and orbits about 36,000 km above the equator in the same sense as the Earth's rotation. For all circular orbits around one planet T^2 is proportional to r^3.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Thermodynamics: First law: dQ = dU + dW, where dW = P dV is the work done by the gas. For an ideal gas dU = n Cv dT and PV = nRT. Always fix the sign convention for heat and work first.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Thermodynamics: Processes: isothermal (T constant, W = nRT ln(V2/V1)), adiabatic (Q = 0, P V^gamma = constant), isobaric (W = P dV) and isochoric (W = 0).

subject: Physics
resource_text: Thermodynamics: Heat engines: efficiency = W/Q_hot = 1 - Q_cold/Q_hot. A Carnot engine between T1 and T2 has the maximum efficiency 1 - T2/T1, with temperatures in kelvin.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Thermodynamics: Calorimetry: heat gained = heat lost in an isolated system. Q = m c dT for a temperature change and Q = m L for a phase change at constant temperature.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Thermodynamics: Ideal gas law PV = nRT with R = 8.31 J/(mol K). Temperatures must be in kelvin: T(K) = T(C) + 273. For a fixed mass of gas P1 V1/T1 = P2 V2/T2.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Thermodynamics: Specific heats of an ideal gas: Cv = f R/2 and Cp = Cv + R, so gamma = Cp/Cv. A monatomic gas has gamma = 5/3 and a diatomic gas has gamma = 7/5.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Thermodynamics: Work in a cyclic process equals the area enclosed on the P-V diagram, positive for a clockwise cycle. The internal energy change over a full cycle is zero, so net heat absorbed = net work done.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Thermodynamics: Latent heat: heat for a phase change Q = m L at constant temperature. The specific heat of water is 4200 J/(kg K), the latent heat of fusion of ice is 336 kJ/kg and of vaporisation is 2260 kJ/kg.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Electrostatics: Coulomb's law F = k q1 q2 / r^2 with k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2. Electric field E = F/q = kq/r^2 for a point charge, directed away from a positive charge. Fields and forces are vectors, so add them with directions.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Electrostatics: Electric potential V = kq/r is a scalar; the potential energy of two charges is U = k q1 q2 / r. Potential difference V = W/q, and E = -dV/dr.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Electrostatics: Gauss's law: flux through a closed surface = q_enclosed / epsilon_0. The field of an infinite line charge is lambda/(2 pi epsilon_0 r) and of an infinite sheet sigma/(2 epsilon_0).

subject: Physics
resource_text: Electrostatics: Capacitors: C = Q/V; parallel plate C = epsilon_0 A / d; stored energy U = (1/2) C V^2. Series: 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2; parallel: C = C1 + C2.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Electrostatics: Fields add as vectors: at the midpoint of two equal like charges the field cancels to zero, but between two equal unlike charges the fields add. Electric field E = F/q = kq/r^2 for a point charge.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Electrostatics: Electric dipole: dipole moment p = q x 2a. Torque in a uniform field tau = p E sin(theta) and potential energy U = -p E cos(theta). The net force on a dipole in a uniform field is zero.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Electrostatics: Capacitors in series: 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2 with equal charge on each; in parallel C = C1 + C2 with equal voltage. A dielectric of constant K multiplies the capacitance by K.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Electrostatics: Charged conducting sphere: E = 0 inside, kQ/r^2 outside and kQ/R^2 at the surface. The potential is constant inside and equal to kQ/R.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Current Electricity: Ohm's law V = I R. Resistivity: R = rho L / A. Series: R = R1 + R2 (same current); parallel: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 (same voltage).

subject: Physics
resource_text: Current Electricity: Kirchhoff's laws: the junction rule (currents into a node sum to zero) and the loop rule (potential changes around a loop sum to zero). Choose a loop direction and track the sign of every emf and IR drop.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Current Electricity: A cell with emf E and internal resistance r gives terminal voltage V = E - I r. Maximum power is delivered to the load when the external resistance equals r.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Current Electricity: Electrical power P = V I = I^2 R = V^2/R; energy E = P t, with 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J. A Wheatstone bridge is balanced when P/Q = R/S, giving zero galvanometer current.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Current Electricity: Resistance R = rho L / A depends on length, cross-section and material. Resistors in series add, R = R1 + R2; in parallel 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2, so the combination is smaller than the smallest resistor.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Current Electricity: A Wheatstone bridge is balanced when P/Q = R/S, so no current flows through the galvanometer. The central branch can then be ignored when simplifying the circuit.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Current Electricity: Drift velocity v_d = I/(n e A) is very small, of the order of mm/s, even though the electric signal travels at nearly the speed of light. Current density J = I/A.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Current Electricity: Cells in series add their emf and internal resistance; n identical cells in parallel give the same emf with internal resistance r/n. Maximum power is delivered to a load when R = r.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Magnetism: Force on a moving charge F = q v B sin(theta), perpendicular to both v and B, so it does no work. In a uniform field a charge moves in a circle of radius r = m v / (q B).

subject: Physics
resource_text: Magnetism: Force on a current-carrying wire F = B I L sin(theta). Field of a long straight wire B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r); at the centre of a circular loop B = mu_0 I / (2R); inside a solenoid B = mu_0 n I.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Magnetism: Faraday's law: induced emf = -d(phi)/dt, and Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change in flux. A rod of length L moving at v in a field B has emf = B L v.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Magnetism: Torque on a current loop tau = N I A B sin(theta); the magnetic moment is M = N I A. Two parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction attract each other.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Magnetism: Field of a long straight wire B = mu0 I/(2 pi r); at the centre of a circular loop B = mu0 I/(2R); inside a long solenoid B = mu0 n I. Here mu0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m/A.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Magnetism: A charged particle moving perpendicular to B follows a circle of radius r = m v/(q B) with period T = 2 pi m/(q B). The period does not depend on the speed.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Magnetism: Motional emf: a rod of length L moving at speed v perpendicular to B gives emf = B L v. Self inductance: emf = -L dI/dt and the energy stored is (1/2) L I^2.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Magnetism: Force between parallel currents per unit length F/L = mu0 I1 I2/(2 pi d): attractive for currents in the same direction and repulsive for opposite directions.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Optics: Mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with f = R/2, using the sign convention where distances are measured from the pole and the direction of incident light is positive. Magnification m = -v/u.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Optics: Lens formula 1/v - 1/u = 1/f; lens maker's formula 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2). Power P = 1/f with f in metres, in dioptres. Thin lenses in contact add their powers.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Optics: Refraction: Snell's law n1 sin(i) = n2 sin(r). Total internal reflection occurs when light goes from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle above the critical angle, sin(C) = n2/n1.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Optics: Young's double slit: fringe width beta = lambda D / d, and bright fringes occur where the path difference is n lambda. Thin film and diffraction patterns follow from the same path-difference reasoning.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Optics: Total internal reflection occurs when light goes from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle above the critical angle, where sin(theta_c) = n_rarer/n_denser. Optical fibres and diamonds use it.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Optics: A prism has refractive index n = sin((A + D_min)/2)/sin(A/2), and for a thin prism the deviation is delta = (n - 1) A. White light disperses because n is larger for violet than for red.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Optics: Power of a lens P = 1/f with f in metres, measured in dioptres. Lenses in contact add their powers: P = P1 + P2. A convex lens has positive power and a concave lens negative power.

subject: Physics
resource_text: Optics: Magnification is m = v/u for lenses and m = -v/u for mirrors, with real inverted images having negative m. Apparent depth = real depth/n for an object seen from the rarer medium.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Mole Concept: One mole contains 6.022 x 10^23 particles (Avogadro's number). Moles = mass / molar mass = number of particles / N_A; for gases at STP, 1 mole occupies 22.4 L.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Mole Concept: Stoichiometry: balance the equation first, then use mole ratios from the coefficients. The limiting reagent is the one that runs out first and decides the amount of product.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Mole Concept: Concentration: molarity M = moles of solute / litres of solution; molality = moles of solute / kg of solvent. Dilution: M1 V1 = M2 V2.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Mole Concept: The empirical formula comes from the simplest mole ratio of the elements; molecular formula = n x empirical formula, where n = molar mass / empirical formula mass.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Mole Concept: Number of moles n = mass/molar mass = number of particles/N_A = volume at STP/22.4 L. At STP one mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 L.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Mole Concept: Limiting reagent: the reactant that gives the least product based on mole ratios. It is not necessarily the one with the smallest mass; divide the moles by the stoichiometric coefficient to compare.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Mole Concept: Percentage composition: % of an element = (mass of the element in one mole of the compound/molar mass) x 100. Percentage yield = actual yield/theoretical yield x 100.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Mole Concept: Dilution: M1 V1 = M2 V2 because the moles of solute stay constant. Mixing solutions of the same solute gives M = (M1 V1 + M2 V2)/(V1 + V2).

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Equilibrium: For aA + bB <-> cC + dD, Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b) using equilibrium concentrations. Pure solids and liquids are left out of K. Kp = Kc (RT)^(delta n).

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Equilibrium: Le Chatelier's principle: a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose any change. Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles; heating favours the endothermic direction; a catalyst changes the rate but not K.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Equilibrium: Reaction quotient Q: if Q < K the reaction goes forward, if Q > K it goes backward and if Q = K it is at equilibrium. K changes only with temperature.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Equilibrium: pH = -log[H+] and pOH = 14 - pH at 25 C. For a weak acid Ka = [H+][A-]/[HA] and alpha = sqrt(Ka/C) for small alpha. Buffer pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]).

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Equilibrium: Relation between Kp and Kc: Kp = Kc (RT)^(delta n), where delta n = moles of gaseous products - moles of gaseous reactants. If delta n = 0 then Kp = Kc.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Equilibrium: Degree of dissociation alpha: for A <-> B + C starting with 1 mol, the total moles at equilibrium are 1 + alpha. Use an ICE table (initial, change, equilibrium) for every problem.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Equilibrium: Solubility product Ksp: for a salt AB with solubility s, Ksp = s^2; for AB2, Ksp = 4 s^3. A precipitate forms when the ionic product exceeds Ksp.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Equilibrium: Buffers resist a change in pH. Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]). For a weak acid alone, pH = (1/2)(pKa - log C).

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Kinetics: Rate law: rate = k [A]^m [B]^n, where the orders m and n come from experiments, not from the balanced equation. Overall order = m + n; the units of k depend on the order.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Kinetics: First-order reaction: ln([A]0/[A]) = k t and half-life t(1/2) = 0.693/k, independent of the initial concentration. Zero-order: [A] = [A]0 - k t and t(1/2) = [A]0/(2k).

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Kinetics: Arrhenius equation k = A e^(-Ea/RT): the rate rises with temperature and falls with higher activation energy. A catalyst lowers Ea and speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Kinetics: Method of initial rates: change one concentration at a time and compare the rates. If doubling [A] doubles the rate the order in A is 1; if it quadruples the rate the order is 2.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Kinetics: Zero-order reaction: [A] = [A]0 - k t and half-life t(1/2) = [A]0/(2k). The rate does not depend on concentration and k has units of mol L^-1 s^-1.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Kinetics: Units of the rate constant for an nth-order reaction are (mol/L)^(1-n) s^-1: first order s^-1, second order L mol^-1 s^-1.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Kinetics: Molecularity is the number of species colliding in an elementary step (1, 2 or 3) and is never zero or fractional, while order is found by experiment and can be fractional. The slowest step is the rate-determining step.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Kinetics: A catalyst lowers the activation energy by giving an alternate path, so it speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally and does not change K or delta H. A 10 degree rise roughly doubles the rate.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Electrochemistry: Cell potential E_cell = E_cathode - E_anode using standard reduction potentials. Reduction happens at the cathode and oxidation at the anode; E_cell > 0 means a spontaneous (galvanic) cell.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Electrochemistry: Nernst equation E = E0 - (0.0592/n) log Q at 25 C. At equilibrium E = 0 and log K = n E0 / 0.0592. Delta G = -n F E.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Electrochemistry: Faraday's laws: mass deposited m = (M I t) / (n F) with F = 96500 C/mol. Charge Q = I t; equivalent mass = molar mass / n.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Electrochemistry: Conductivity kappa = 1/rho; molar conductivity = kappa x 1000 / M. Kohlrausch's law: the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the contributions of its ions.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Electrochemistry: Gibbs energy and cell potential: delta G0 = -n F E0cell, and E0cell = (0.0591/n) log K at 298 K. A positive E0cell means a spontaneous reaction.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Electrochemistry: Electrolysis products: at the cathode the species with the higher reduction potential is reduced; at the anode the species with the lower reduction potential is oxidised. In aqueous NaCl, H2 forms at the cathode and Cl2 at the anode.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Electrochemistry: Kohlrausch's law: the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the contributions of its ions. Molar conductivity increases on dilution because dissociation and ion mobility increase.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Electrochemistry: One mole of electrons carries 96500 C and Q = I t. For the same charge, the masses deposited are in the ratio of their equivalent weights.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Bonding: Bond formation follows the octet rule (with exceptions); VSEPR theory predicts molecular geometry from the electron pairs around the central atom: 2 pairs linear, 3 trigonal planar, 4 tetrahedral. Lone pairs squeeze the bond angles.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Bonding: Hybridisation: sp (linear, 180 degrees), sp2 (trigonal planar, 120 degrees), sp3 (tetrahedral, 109.5 degrees). Count sigma bonds plus lone pairs on the central atom to find the hybridisation.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Bonding: Molecular orbital theory: bond order = (bonding electrons - antibonding electrons)/2. A higher bond order means a shorter, stronger bond; O2 is paramagnetic because of two unpaired electrons.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Bonding: Ionic bonds form by electron transfer and covalent bonds by sharing. Polarity depends on electronegativity difference and shape; dipole moments cancel in symmetric molecules like CO2 and CCl4. Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded to N, O or F.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Bonding: Dipole moment mu = q x d. Symmetrical molecules such as CO2, BF3 and CCl4 are non-polar even though their bonds are polar, while H2O and NH3 are polar.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Bonding: Hydrogen bonding occurs when H is bonded to N, O or F. It raises boiling points (H2O vs H2S); intramolecular H-bonding (o-nitrophenol) lowers the boiling point compared with intermolecular H-bonding (p-nitrophenol).

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Bonding: Bond order from MO theory: O2 has bond order 2 and is paramagnetic, N2 has bond order 3 and is diamagnetic. A higher bond order means a shorter and stronger bond.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Chemical Bonding: Formal charge = valence electrons - non-bonding electrons - (1/2) bonding electrons. The real molecule is a resonance hybrid, e.g. all C-O bonds in the carbonate ion are equal.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Periodic Properties: Atomic radius decreases across a period (rising nuclear charge) and increases down a group (more shells). Cations are smaller and anions larger than their parent atoms.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Periodic Properties: Ionisation energy generally increases across a period and decreases down a group, with exceptions: Be > B and N > O because of filled and half-filled subshell stability.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Periodic Properties: Electronegativity rises across a period and falls down a group (fluorine is highest). Electron gain enthalpy is most negative for chlorine, not fluorine, because of fluorine's small size and electron repulsion.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Periodic Properties: Isoelectronic species have the same number of electrons; their size decreases as the nuclear charge increases (N3- > O2- > F- > Na+ > Mg2+). Diagonal relationships exist between Li-Mg and Be-Al.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Periodic Properties: Electron gain enthalpy is most negative for chlorine, not fluorine, because fluorine's small size causes strong electron-electron repulsion. Noble gases have positive values.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Periodic Properties: Exceptions in ionisation energy: Be is higher than B because of the stable filled 2s subshell, and N is higher than O because of the half-filled 2p3 configuration. Check subshell stability before applying the general trend.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Periodic Properties: The group number gives the maximum oxidation state of a main-group element. Diagonal pairs Li-Mg, Be-Al and B-Si show similar properties.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Periodic Properties: Metallic character increases down a group and decreases across a period. Oxides change from basic on the left to acidic on the right, with Al2O3 being amphoteric.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Coordination Compounds: A complex has a central metal ion bonded to ligands. The coordination number is the number of ligand donor atoms attached. Oxidation state of the metal = overall charge minus the sum of the ligand charges.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Coordination Compounds: Naming: list ligands first in alphabetical order, then the metal with its oxidation state in roman numerals; anionic complexes end in -ate. [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 is hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Coordination Compounds: Crystal field theory: an octahedral field splits the d orbitals into t2g (lower) and eg (higher). Strong-field ligands such as CN- give low-spin complexes and weak-field ligands like Cl- give high-spin complexes.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Coordination Compounds: Isomerism: structural (ionisation, linkage, coordination) and stereo (geometrical cis-trans and optical). Magnetic moment = sqrt(n(n+2)) BM for n unpaired electrons.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Coordination Compounds: The coordination number is the number of donor atoms bonded to the metal. Four gives tetrahedral or square planar, six gives octahedral. Ligands can be monodentate (Cl-, NH3), bidentate (en, ox) or polydentate (EDTA).

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Coordination Compounds: The oxidation state of the metal = overall charge of the complex - sum of the ligand charges. In K4[Fe(CN)6] the iron is +2.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Coordination Compounds: Spin-only magnetic moment = sqrt(n(n + 2)) BM where n is the number of unpaired electrons. Strong field ligands (CN-, CO) give low-spin complexes; weak field ligands (halides, H2O) give high spin.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Coordination Compounds: Colour arises from d-d transitions between the split d levels; d0 and d10 ions are usually colourless. Chelate complexes are more stable than those of monodentate ligands (the chelate effect).

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Hydrocarbons: Alkanes (CnH2n+2) undergo free-radical substitution; alkenes (CnH2n) and alkynes (CnH2n-2) undergo electrophilic addition. Markovnikov's rule: the hydrogen adds to the carbon that already has more hydrogens.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Hydrocarbons: IUPAC naming: choose the longest carbon chain, number from the end that gives the lowest locants to substituents or double bonds, and list substituents alphabetically.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Hydrocarbons: Benzene is aromatic (Huckel rule: 4n + 2 pi electrons) and prefers electrophilic substitution (nitration, halogenation, Friedel-Crafts) over addition because it keeps its stable delocalised ring.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Hydrocarbons: Combustion of CxHy needs (x + y/4) moles of O2 per mole and gives x CO2 and y/2 H2O. Alkenes decolourise bromine water and Baeyer's reagent, which distinguishes them from alkanes.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Hydrocarbons: Markovnikov's rule: in the addition of HX to an unsymmetrical alkene the hydrogen goes to the carbon that already has more hydrogens, giving the more stable carbocation. In the presence of peroxide, HBr adds in the anti-Markovnikov way.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Hydrocarbons: Terminal alkynes (R-C triple bond C-H) have an acidic hydrogen and react with sodamide or ammoniacal silver nitrate to give acetylides, while alkenes and internal alkynes do not.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Hydrocarbons: Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution: nitration with conc. HNO3 and conc. H2SO4 gives nitrobenzene, and Friedel-Crafts alkylation uses RCl with AlCl3. The ring keeps its aromaticity.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Hydrocarbons: Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C bond to give carbonyl compounds; with Zn/H2O, RCH=CHR' gives RCHO and R'CHO. Hydrogenation over Ni, Pd or Pt gives the alkane.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: General Organic Chemistry: Inductive effect: electron-withdrawing groups (-NO2, -Cl) pull electron density through sigma bonds, while alkyl groups push it (+I). The resonance (mesomeric) effect delocalises pi electrons and stabilises ions.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: General Organic Chemistry: Stability of intermediates: carbocation 3 degree > 2 degree > 1 degree > methyl (hyperconjugation and +I); carbanion stability follows the reverse order; free radicals follow the carbocation order.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: General Organic Chemistry: Acidity and basicity: a stronger acid has a more stable conjugate base. Electron-withdrawing groups increase the acidity of carboxylic acids; amines are basic because of the lone pair on nitrogen.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: General Organic Chemistry: Isomerism: structural isomers differ in connectivity and stereoisomers differ in spatial arrangement. A carbon with four different groups is a chiral centre, and n such centres give up to 2^n stereoisomers.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: General Organic Chemistry: Resonance and mesomeric effect: +M groups (-OH, -NH2) donate electrons into the ring, activating the ortho and para positions; -M groups (-NO2, -CHO) withdraw electrons and direct to the meta position.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: General Organic Chemistry: Hyperconjugation: the number of alpha C-H bonds stabilises carbocations and alkenes. More alpha hydrogens means greater stability, so (CH3)3C+ is more stable than CH3CH2+.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: General Organic Chemistry: Nucleophiles are electron-rich (OH-, CN-, NH3) and electrophiles electron-poor (H+, carbocations, BF3). SN1 occurs for tertiary halides via a carbocation and racemisation; SN2 occurs for primary halides with inversion.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: General Organic Chemistry: Optical isomerism: a carbon with four different groups is chiral and gives two enantiomers. n chiral centres give up to 2^n stereoisomers, but a meso compound is achiral despite having chiral centres.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Aldehydes and Ketones: The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic, so both undergo nucleophilic addition; aldehydes are more reactive than ketones because of less steric hindrance and less electron donation.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Aldehydes and Ketones: Tests: Tollens' reagent (silver mirror) and Fehling's solution (red precipitate) are given by aldehydes but not by ketones. The iodoform test is positive for methyl ketones and for ethanol.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Aldehydes and Ketones: Aldol condensation occurs with aldehydes or ketones that have alpha hydrogens, in dilute base. The Cannizzaro reaction: aldehydes without alpha hydrogen (HCHO, benzaldehyde) disproportionate in concentrated base.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Aldehydes and Ketones: Preparation: oxidation of primary alcohols gives aldehydes and of secondary alcohols gives ketones; ozonolysis of alkenes gives carbonyl compounds. NaBH4 or LiAlH4 reduce them back to alcohols.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Aldehydes and Ketones: Reactivity towards nucleophilic addition: aldehydes are more reactive than ketones because of less steric hindrance and a more positive carbonyl carbon, so HCHO > CH3CHO > CH3COCH3.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Aldehydes and Ketones: Cannizzaro reaction: aldehydes with no alpha hydrogen (HCHO, benzaldehyde) on heating with concentrated NaOH undergo disproportionation to give an alcohol and a carboxylate salt.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Aldehydes and Ketones: Iodoform test: compounds containing CH3-CO- or CH3-CH(OH)- give a yellow precipitate of CHI3 with I2 and NaOH. Ethanal and propanone respond, but methanal and 3-pentanone do not.

subject: Chemistry
resource_text: Aldehydes and Ketones: Reduction: NaBH4 or LiAlH4 reduce aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols; Clemmensen (Zn-Hg/HCl) and Wolff-Kishner (NH2NH2/KOH) reduce C=O to CH2.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Quadratic Equations: For ax^2 + bx + c = 0, the roots are (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / 2a. The discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac decides the nature of the roots: D > 0 two distinct real roots, D = 0 equal roots, D < 0 complex roots.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Quadratic Equations: Sum of roots = -b/a and product of roots = c/a. A quadratic with roots p and q is x^2 - (p + q)x + pq = 0. Symmetric expressions follow, e.g. p^2 + q^2 = (p + q)^2 - 2pq.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Quadratic Equations: For a > 0 the minimum value of ax^2 + bx + c occurs at x = -b/(2a) and equals -D/(4a); for a < 0 this is the maximum. The parabola opens upward when a > 0.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Quadratic Equations: To test roots in an interval or common roots of two quadratics, eliminate the shared root. For inequalities sketch the parabola and read off the sign of each region.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Quadratic Equations: With real coefficients, complex roots come in conjugate pairs. If the coefficients are rational and D is a perfect square the roots are rational; if D is positive but not a perfect square the roots are irrational conjugates.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Quadratic Equations: ax^2 + bx + c > 0 for all x when a > 0 and D < 0. A quadratic has both roots positive when the sum is positive, the product is positive and D >= 0.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Quadratic Equations: Equations reducible to quadratics: put y = x^2 for biquadratics or t = x + 1/x for reciprocal equations, and always check the solutions in the original equation for extraneous roots.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Quadratic Equations: Cube roots of unity are 1, w and w^2 with 1 + w + w^2 = 0 and w^3 = 1. The complex roots of x^2 + x + 1 = 0 are w and w^2.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Sequences and Series: Arithmetic progression: nth term a_n = a + (n - 1)d and sum S_n = (n/2)(2a + (n - 1)d) = (n/2)(a + l).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Sequences and Series: Geometric progression: a_n = a r^(n-1), S_n = a(r^n - 1)/(r - 1), and the sum to infinity S = a/(1 - r) exists only when |r| < 1.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Sequences and Series: Means: AM >= GM >= HM for positive numbers, with equality only when all the numbers are equal. For two numbers GM^2 = AM x HM. Useful for maximum and minimum problems.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Sequences and Series: Standard sums: 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2, the sum of squares = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 and the sum of cubes = [n(n+1)/2]^2. Telescoping splits terms such as 1/(k(k+1)) = 1/k - 1/(k+1).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Sequences and Series: The sum of an infinite GP is S = a/(1 - r) provided |r| < 1. If |r| >= 1 the sum does not exist.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Sequences and Series: If a, b, c are in AP then 2b = a + c, and if they are in GP then b^2 = a c. Three terms in AP can be taken as a - d, a, a + d.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Sequences and Series: Telescoping series: write 1/(n(n + 1)) = 1/n - 1/(n + 1) so that the sum of n terms collapses to 1 - 1/(n + 1).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Sequences and Series: For two numbers, AM = (a + b)/2 and GM = sqrt(ab). If the AM and GM are given, the numbers are the roots of x^2 - 2(AM)x + GM^2 = 0. Inserting n arithmetic means between a and b gives common difference d = (b - a)/(n + 1).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Permutations and Combinations: Fundamental principle: if one task can be done in m ways and another in n ways, doing both gives m x n ways (m + n for either/or). nPr = n!/(n-r)! counts ordered arrangements and nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!) counts selections.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Permutations and Combinations: Arrangements with repeated items: n!/(p! q! ...). Circular arrangements of n objects: (n-1)!. For 'together' restrictions treat the items as one block and multiply by their internal arrangements.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Permutations and Combinations: Conditional selections: use complement counting (total minus unwanted) and nCr = nC(n-r). Ways to distribute n identical items among r people is (n+r-1)C(r-1).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Permutations and Combinations: The binomial theorem: (x + y)^n has n + 1 terms and the general term is nCr x^(n-r) y^r. Inclusion-exclusion handles 'at least one' and 'none in its place' problems.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Permutations and Combinations: nPr = n!/(n - r)! and nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!). Also nCr = nC(n - r) and nCr + nC(r - 1) = (n + 1)Cr.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Permutations and Combinations: Circular arrangements of n distinct objects = (n - 1)!, and (n - 1)!/2 if clockwise and anticlockwise are the same (necklaces).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Permutations and Combinations: Dividing n distinct objects into groups of sizes p and q gives n!/(p! q!); if the groups have equal size, divide further by the factorial of the number of equal groups.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Permutations and Combinations: For objects that must stay together, treat them as one block and then multiply by their internal arrangements. For objects that must not be together, use total minus together.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Probability: P(E) = favourable outcomes / total equally likely outcomes. P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B) and P(not A) = 1 - P(A).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Probability: Conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B). Independent events satisfy P(A and B) = P(A) P(B). Do not confuse mutually exclusive events with independent events.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Probability: Bayes' theorem: P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A) / P(B), where P(B) comes from the total probability theorem over all cases. Draw a tree diagram to keep the cases organised.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Probability: Binomial distribution: the probability of exactly r successes in n independent trials is nCr p^r (1-p)^(n-r). Mean = np and variance = np(1-p).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Probability: Addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). For mutually exclusive events the last term is zero. Complement: P(not A) = 1 - P(A).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Probability: Independent events satisfy P(A and B) = P(A) P(B). Do not confuse independent with mutually exclusive: mutually exclusive events with nonzero probabilities are never independent.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Probability: The expected value of a random variable is E(X) = sum of x p(x). For a binomial distribution the mean is np and the variance is npq.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Probability: Drawing without replacement changes the probabilities after each draw, so multiply conditional probabilities or use combinations: P = (favourable combinations)/(total combinations).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Straight Lines: Slope m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1) = tan(theta). Equation forms: y = mx + c, point-slope y - y1 = m(x - x1), intercept form x/a + y/b = 1 and general form ax + by + c = 0.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Straight Lines: The distance of the point (x1, y1) from the line ax + by + c = 0 is |a x1 + b y1 + c| / sqrt(a^2 + b^2). The distance between parallel lines uses the same formula on their constants.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Straight Lines: Parallel lines have equal slopes and perpendicular lines have m1 m2 = -1. The angle between two lines satisfies tan(theta) = |(m1 - m2)/(1 + m1 m2)|.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Straight Lines: Section formula: the point dividing (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) in ratio m:n internally is ((m x2 + n x1)/(m+n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m+n)). The area of a triangle comes from a determinant of the coordinates.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Straight Lines: Forms of a line: slope-intercept y = mx + c, point-slope y - y1 = m(x - x1), two-point form, and intercept form x/a + y/b = 1.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Straight Lines: The angle between two lines with slopes m1 and m2 satisfies tan(theta) = |(m1 - m2)/(1 + m1 m2)|. The lines are perpendicular when m1 m2 = -1.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Straight Lines: The distance between parallel lines ax + by + c1 = 0 and ax + by + c2 = 0 is |c1 - c2|/sqrt(a^2 + b^2). The coefficients of x and y must be the same before applying the formula.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Straight Lines: The area of a triangle with vertices (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (x3, y3) is (1/2)|x1(y2 - y3) + x2(y3 - y1) + x3(y1 - y2)|. Three points are collinear when the area is zero.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Circles: Standard form (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2 with centre (h, k). The general form x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (-g, -f) and radius sqrt(g^2 + f^2 - c).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Circles: A line is tangent to a circle when its perpendicular distance from the centre equals the radius. The length of the tangent from an external point P is sqrt(S1), found by substituting P into the circle equation.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Circles: Two circles touch externally if the distance between the centres equals r1 + r2, and internally if it equals |r1 - r2|. The radical axis of two circles is S1 - S2 = 0.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Circles: The tangent at (x1, y1) on x^2 + y^2 = a^2 is x x1 + y y1 = a^2. The normal at that point passes through the centre.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Circles: The general form x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (-g, -f) and radius sqrt(g^2 + f^2 - c). It represents a real circle only if g^2 + f^2 - c > 0.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Circles: The length of the tangent from an external point (x1, y1) is sqrt(S1), where S1 = x1^2 + y1^2 + 2g x1 + 2f y1 + c. The point is inside, on or outside the circle according as S1 < 0, = 0 or > 0.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Circles: The circle with endpoints of a diameter at (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is (x - x1)(x - x2) + (y - y1)(y - y2) = 0.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Circles: The perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord, so the chord length is 2 sqrt(r^2 - d^2), where d is the distance of the chord from the centre.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Trigonometric Equations: Principal solutions: sin x = sin a gives x = n pi + (-1)^n a; cos x = cos a gives x = 2 n pi +/- a; tan x = tan a gives x = n pi + a, where n is any integer.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Trigonometric Equations: Identities: sin^2 x + cos^2 x = 1, sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x, cos 2x = 1 - 2 sin^2 x = 2 cos^2 x - 1. Reduce an equation to a single trigonometric function before solving.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Trigonometric Equations: Equations of the form a sin x + b cos x = c: write the left side as R sin(x + alpha) with R = sqrt(a^2 + b^2); a solution exists only if |c| <= R.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Trigonometric Equations: Always check the given interval, and reject solutions that make a denominator or a tangent undefined. Sum to product: sin A + sin B = 2 sin((A+B)/2) cos((A-B)/2).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Trigonometric Equations: Compound angles: sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B, cos(A + B) = cos A cos B - sin A sin B, tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 - tan A tan B).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Trigonometric Equations: Sum to product: sin A + sin B = 2 sin((A + B)/2) cos((A - B)/2) and cos A + cos B = 2 cos((A + B)/2) cos((A - B)/2). Use them to factorise equations.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Trigonometric Equations: tan x = tan a has general solution x = n pi + a, and sin^2 x = sin^2 a gives x = n pi +/- a. Do not divide both sides by a trigonometric factor, as that can lose solutions.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Trigonometric Equations: Standard values: sin 30 = 1/2, sin 45 = 1/sqrt(2), sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2 and tan 45 = 1. Double angle: cos 2x = 2 cos^2 x - 1 = 1 - 2 sin^2 x.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Limits and Derivatives: Standard limits: lim x->0 sin x / x = 1, lim x->0 (e^x - 1)/x = 1 and lim x->0 (1 + x)^(1/x) = e. For 0/0 forms factorise, rationalise, or apply L'Hopital's rule.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Limits and Derivatives: Differentiation rules: product (uv)' = u'v + uv', quotient (u/v)' = (u'v - uv')/v^2, chain rule d/dx f(g(x)) = f'(g(x)) g'(x). Also d/dx sin x = cos x and d/dx e^x = e^x.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Limits and Derivatives: Maxima and minima: set f'(x) = 0 to find the critical points; f''(x) < 0 gives a maximum and f''(x) > 0 gives a minimum. Check the end points for a closed interval.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Limits and Derivatives: The slope of the tangent to y = f(x) at x = a is f'(a), and the tangent line is y - f(a) = f'(a)(x - a). A function is increasing where f'(x) > 0.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Limits and Derivatives: L'Hopital's rule: if a limit gives 0/0 or infinity/infinity, differentiate the numerator and denominator separately and take the limit again. Check for the indeterminate form first.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Limits and Derivatives: Chain rule: d/dx f(g(x)) = f'(g(x)) g'(x). Standard derivatives: d/dx sin x = cos x, d/dx e^x = e^x, d/dx ln x = 1/x, d/dx tan x = sec^2 x.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Limits and Derivatives: Continuity at x = a needs the left limit, the right limit and f(a) to be equal. A function differentiable at a point is continuous there, but not conversely (|x| at 0).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Limits and Derivatives: Related rates: dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt). A function is increasing where f'(x) > 0 and decreasing where f'(x) < 0.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Integration: Standard integrals: the integral of x^n dx is x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C (n not equal to -1), of 1/x dx is ln|x| + C, of e^x dx is e^x + C and of sin x dx is -cos x + C. Never forget the constant C for an indefinite integral.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Integration: Substitution: let u = g(x) and replace dx. Integration by parts: the integral of u dv = u v - the integral of v du, choosing u by the order ILATE (Inverse, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Integration: Definite integrals: the integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a). Area under a curve is the integral of f(x) when f >= 0; split the interval wherever the curve crosses the axis.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Integration: Properties: the integral from a to b of f(x) dx equals the integral from a to b of f(a + b - x) dx; for odd functions over [-a, a] the integral is 0, and for even functions it is twice the integral over [0, a].

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Integration: Integration by parts: integral of u dv = u v - integral of v du. Choose u by the order inverse trig, logarithm, algebraic, trig, exponential (ILATE).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Integration: Partial fractions: split 1/((x - a)(x - b)) into A/(x - a) + B/(x - b) before integrating. Standard form: integral of 1/(x^2 + a^2) dx = (1/a) tan^-1(x/a) + C.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Integration: The area under a curve between x = a and x = b is the integral of |y| dx; for areas below the axis take the positive value. The area between curves is the integral of (upper - lower).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Integration: Useful integrals: integral of 1/x dx = ln|x| + C, integral of e^(ax) dx = e^(ax)/a + C, integral of sin x dx = -cos x + C, integral of sec^2 x dx = tan x + C.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Vectors: Dot product a.b = |a||b| cos(theta) = a1b1 + a2b2 + a3b3; it is zero for perpendicular vectors. Cross product |a x b| = |a||b| sin(theta) gives a vector perpendicular to both, and a x b = -(b x a).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Vectors: Magnitude |a| = sqrt(a1^2 + a2^2 + a3^2) and the unit vector is a/|a|. The projection of a on b is (a.b)/|b|. Two vectors are parallel if one is a scalar multiple of the other.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Vectors: The area of a parallelogram with adjacent sides a and b is |a x b| and the triangle has half of that. The scalar triple product [a b c] = a.(b x c) gives the volume of the parallelepiped.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Vectors: The position vector of the point dividing a and b in ratio m:n is (m b + n a)/(m + n). Three points are collinear if one displacement vector is a scalar multiple of another.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Vectors: The cross product a x b = |a||b| sin(theta) n is perpendicular to both vectors. In components it is the determinant of i, j, k with the components of a and b, and a x b = -(b x a).

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Vectors: The scalar triple product [a b c] = a . (b x c) is the volume of the parallelepiped. The vectors are coplanar when it is zero.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Vectors: The projection of a on b is (a . b)/|b|, and the angle between two vectors satisfies cos(theta) = (a . b)/(|a||b|). The vectors are perpendicular when the dot product is zero.

subject: Mathematics
resource_text: Vectors: Points A, B, C are collinear if AB = k AC for some scalar k. A unit vector in the direction of a is a/|a|.
